title: The gamification dilemma in education: A compromise model between extrinsic motivation and existential well-being
abstract: Context and relevance. Gamification is widely introduced into higher education as a means of enhancing academic motivation, yet its effects are contradictory: short-term gains in engagement are often accompanied by increased anxiety, burnout, and alienation. Existing approaches assess effectiveness mainly through instrumental metrics, ignoring students' subjective experiences and existential well-being. This contradiction and the theoretical vacuum around it determine the relevance of the study. Objective. To identify the contradiction between extrinsic motivation and the existential well-being of students in a gamified environment and to develop a theoretical compromise model. Hypothesis. The gamification dilemma is a systemic property arising from the contradiction between the external nature of its stimuli and the internal conditions of well-being; there are “critical points” in the design, the management of which allows a compromise to be found. Methods and materials. The study involved 180 undergraduate students of Lipetsk State Technical University (age 18–23, M = 20,2; SD = 1,3; 60% female), selected by purposive convenience sampling through the online platform Yandex Forms, who systematically encountered elements of gamification in their academic courses. The authors' scales for assessing the perception of gamification elements were used, along with validated questionnaires on academic motivation, anxiety, impostor syndrome, and academic cynicism. Results. The key predictor of increased anxiety, impostor syndrome, and learning disengagement is the subjective perception of gamification as a system of external control, rather than its mere presence; public comparison and the perception of bonus points as a mandatory race are the most destructive. Conclusions. The gamification dilemma has been empirically confirmed. The developed model identifies an “incompatibility zone”, a “managed compromise zone”, and four “critical points” for design. It is recommended to redesign educational environments, shifting the focus from external control to supporting students' autonomy, competence, and meaningfulness.
